title: Checkpoint: Power for the World
objective: After this level you can compare the main ways the world makes electricity and their trade-offs.
summary: In 2025 coal and renewables each made about a third of the world's electricity, gas about a fifth. Each source trades off carbon, waste and weather, and one grid carries them all.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: where did the world's electricity come from in 2025?
cards.body: About a third came from burning coal. About another third came from renewables: water, wind, sunlight and more. Gas made about a fifth. Every source in this chapter is in that mix, and each one is a trade-off. Time to line them up.

items.label: Burn fuel
points: Coal and gas boil water to spin turbines (Level 12)

items.label: Split atoms
points: Nuclear heat makes steam, with no CO2 while running (Level 14)
Spent fuel stays dangerous for thousands of years

items.label: Catch nature
points: Water, wind and sun burn nothing (Levels 15–17)
Output depends on river flow, wind speed and daylight, so storage helps (Level 18)

cards.fact: In 2025, more than 40% of the world's electricity came from low-emissions sources.
cards.context: That's renewables plus nuclear, by the International Energy Agency's count. Coal still made about a third on its own. And almost every source still ends the same way: something spins a turbine, and the turbine spins Level 8's generator. Solar panels are the big exception, with nothing spinning at all.

cards.headline: Then they all share one road
cards.body: However it's made, electricity then takes Level 11's trip: stepped up to as much as 765,000 volts, carried across the grid, and stepped down to 120 or 240 volts at your home. All the while, operators keep supply matching demand, every moment, whichever sources are running.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: How most power plants are giant kettles: heat from fuel or atoms boils water and steam spins a turbine.
How wind, water and sunlight make power, and why doubling wind speed gives eight times the power.
Why each power source trades off carbon, waste and weather, and why coal emits the most per kilowatt-hour.
Why the grid must match supply and demand every moment, and how storage shifts power to when it's needed.

questions.prompt: In 2025, roughly what share of the world's electricity came from coal?

options.label: About two-thirds
options.rationale: Coal made about a third, not two-thirds.

options.label: Nearly all of it
options.rationale: Renewables alone made about a third.

questions.explanation: Coal made about 34% of the world's electricity in 2025, about the same as all renewables together.

questions.prompt: Power for the World recap: which source makes electricity without spinning any turbine?

options.label: Wind power
options.rationale: The wind spins a rotor and generator.

questions.explanation: Solar cells turn sunlight straight into current: electrons knocked loose in a semiconductor. Nothing spins.

questions.prompt: Power for the World recap: why does a grid with lots of solar power need storage?

options.label: Stored midday solar covers times the sun isn't shining
Solar panels make an AC the grid can't use
options.rationale: Panels make DC, and inverters convert it.

options.label: Storage makes solar panels more efficient
options.rationale: Storage shifts energy in time; it doesn't change the panels.

options.label: Solar power must be used within a second or it's lost forever
options.rationale: Batteries can hold it for hours.

questions.explanation: Batteries charge on extra midday solar and release it in the evening, when the sun isn't shining.

questions.prompt: In Level 19's debate over the energy path, what does Greenpeace call for?

options.label: A fast, fair phase-out of coal, oil and gas
Replacing wind farms with gas plants
options.rationale: Greenpeace wants fossil fuels phased out.

questions.explanation: Greenpeace calls for a fast and fair phase-out of fossil fuels; OPEC stresses continued oil investment.

questions.prompt: Power for the World recap: why do wind turbines stand on such tall towers?

options.label: To keep the blades out of people's reach
options.rationale: Height is about the wind, not safety.

options.label: Because wind is generally faster higher up
Because tall towers store energy
options.rationale: Towers hold turbines up; they don't store energy.

questions.explanation: Wind speeds are generally higher farther above the ground, and power rises with the cube of wind speed.
